name: The Donation of Constantine
plain_explanation: A document forged by churchmen, probably around the time of Pepin's gift of Italian territory to the Pope, claiming that the Emperor Constantine had given Pope Sylvester and his successors dominion over Rome and the whole Western Empire when Constantine moved his capital East. It was believed genuine throughout the Middle Ages and used to justify the Pope's temporal power over the Papal States.
precise_definition: A forged imperial decree, accepted as authentic until Lorenzo Valla's philological exposure of it as a fabrication in 1439, that served as the legal-historical basis for papal claims to temporal sovereignty in Italy.
why_it_mattered: It gave 'an air of antique legality' to Pepin's eighth-century donation of Ravenna and the Exarchate, illustrating the medieval habit of legitimizing new arrangements through fabricated appeals to ancient authority.
historical_origin: Forged in connection with Pepin's donation to the papacy (754), to make the Pope's temporal possessions appear to derive from imperial grant rather than mere Frankish military conquest.
examples: C. Delisle Burns's summary of its fantastical narrative: Constantine's leprosy, his vision of Peter and Paul, his baptism by Sylvester, and his supposed grant of 'Rome and all the provinces...of Italy and the West' to the Roman Church
objections: Lorenzo Valla's 1439 philological demonstration that its Latin could not be genuine fourth-century usage
influence_on_later_thinkers: Even after being exposed as a forgery, Pope Nicholas V (who made Valla his secretary) did not relinquish the States of the Church whose title had rested on it.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly underwrites the Church's claim to temporal, not merely spiritual, sovereignty in central Italy.
